games.title: Brogue
games.subtitle: Community Edition
games.description: A luminous, tightly designed dungeon dive: twenty-six levels, no experience points, and every item a decision. Find the Amulet of Yendor at the bottom.
about: Brogue was created by Brian Walker and is now maintained by the community as Brogue: Community Edition. It strips the classic roguelike down to its essentials—no classes, no grinding—and builds its depth from item identification, allies, terrain and light.

This port compiles the official Brogue CE source to WebAssembly without changing any game code. The screen is drawn from Brogue's own tile sheet in text, tiles or hybrid mode, and the game's keyboard and mouse controls work exactly as on the desktop.
games.rationale: First implementation: validates tile rendering, map interaction, touch controls and responsive gameplay.
games.authors: Brian Walker; Brogue: Community Edition contributors

license.assets: Tile sheet: CC BY-SA 4.0 (Brogue CE maintainers, based on Oryx Design Lab tiles distributed with Brogue under the AGPL)

cover.alt: Brogue in tiles mode: the adventurer in a torch-lit dungeon with the stats sidebar on the left.

knownLimitations: Played through on a physical iPhone (iOS Safari) in November 2026; not yet tested on Android devices, Firefox or desktop Safari.
Phones use a rearranged layout (full-screen map, status bar, menus as large sheets); pinch to resize the map. Tablets and desktop show Brogue's original screen.
iPhone Safari cannot hide its toolbars from a web page; add the site to the Home Screen for a full-screen view.
The tile downscaler is a simplified version of Brogue's desktop renderer (no sub-pixel sharpening or wall-top shading), so very small sizes can look softer than on desktop.
Screenshots (the desktop build's Print Screen command) are not supported in the browser.

compatibility.notes: New game, movement, save, reload and load verified by end-to-end tests.

Phone layout, thumb pad, context dock (stairs route, search, eat, targeting, recording playback), long-press fans, sheets, drawer and on-screen keyboard exercised by end-to-end tests; not a substitute for a real device.
Played on a physical iPhone (iOS Safari) in November 2026: playable, with the touch controls. Desktop Safari not yet tested.

games.title: Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup
games.subtitle: The community-developed classic
games.description: A deep, open-source dungeon crawl with dozens of species and backgrounds, a sprawling branch structure and a design culture of removing tedium.
games.rationale: Second implementation: validates terminal and tiles interfaces, complex prompts, menus, targeting and command handling.
games.authors: The Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup development team

license.code: GPL-2.0-or-later (with bundled Lua (MIT), SQLite (public domain), PCRE (BSD), zlib (zlib) and jQuery/RequireJS (MIT) in the browser client)
license.assets: Tiles: CC0 1.0 (DCSS tiles project); fonts: DejaVu (free license)

about: Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup grew out of Linley's Dungeon Crawl and has been developed in the open by a large volunteer team since 2006. It is known for its many species, backgrounds and gods, a branching dungeon, and a design philosophy that removes tedium rather than adding it.

This port compiles the official DCSS source to WebAssembly without changing any game code, and shows it with DCSS's own WebTiles client, the same one the official online servers use. It runs entirely in your browser: no server and no account.

DCSS only tells whether a character has spells inside its menus: the phone dock leads with Cast until the game has said there are none, then with Ability.
No sound (DCSS's browser interface has none).

compatibility.notes: New character, auto-explore, menus, message log, save, reload and continue verified by end-to-end tests.

Phone layout, status drawer, character creation by tap, context docks (stairs button, look, travel menu, combat dock when a monster is in view), latches and long-press fans exercised by end-to-end tests; not a substitute for a real device.

games.title: Sil-Q
games.subtitle: Tactical descent into Angband
games.description: A tactical roguelike set in Tolkien's First Age, where stealth, positioning and a single run to steal a Silmaril matter more than loot.
games.rationale: Distinct tactical roguelike; existing browser/WASM work provides a useful starting point.
games.authors: Sil-Q maintainers, building on Sil by half and Kanga

license.code: GPL-2.0-only (Sil-Q is dual-licensed: GPL-2.0 or the Angband licence; distributed here under GPL-2.0)
license.assets: No graphics, sounds or fonts are shipped: the game is drawn as text with the browser's monospace font

about: Sil is a tactical roguelike by half and Kanga, set in Tolkien's First Age: you descend into Morgoth's fortress of Angband to steal a Silmaril from his crown. There is no town and no shopping; experience comes largely from discovery rather than killing, and stealth, light, positioning and a strong combat model decide fights. Sil-Q is the community continuation of Sil.

This port compiles the official Sil-Q source to WebAssembly without changing any game code; only a browser display module is added, as upstream has for curses, X11, Windows and macOS. It runs entirely in your browser: no server and no account.

games.title: Rogue
games.subtitle: 5.4.4 source release
games.description: The game that named the genre: explore the Dungeons of Doom, identify what you find, and bring back the Amulet of Yendor.
games.rationale: Small, classic terminal roguelike; relatively straightforward integration.
games.authors: Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold; 5.4.4 source release by the Roguelike Restoration Project

license.code: BSD-3-Clause (Rogue 5.4.4 source release; state.c and mdport.c by Nicholas J. Kisseberth, xcrypt.c by David Burren, under the same terms)
license.assets: Optional tiles: CC0 1.0 (Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup's tile export, based on the public-domain RLTiles; Kenney's 1-Bit Pack); otherwise text in the browser's monospace font

cover.alt: Rogue in text mode: the adventurer, shown as @, meets an emu (E) in a lit room with food and gold; a passage leads away below.

about: Rogue is the 1980 game that named the genre: descend through the Dungeons of Doom, identify potions, scrolls, rings and wands by trying them, and bring back the Amulet of Yendor. Every level is new, every death is final, and the screen is made of letters.

This port compiles the Rogue 5.4.4 source release, the later BSD-licensed version, without changing it, on a small curses written for the browser. It runs entirely in your browser: no server and no account.

As in the original, Rogue saves only when you press S, and a saved game is removed when you continue it: closing the page mid-game loses that game's progress.
No shell escape (!): there is no shell in the browser.

games.title: HyperRogue
games.subtitle: A roguelike in non-Euclidean space
games.description: Collect treasure on a hyperbolic plane, where the world grows exponentially around you and geometry is the main puzzle.
games.rationale: Unusual non-Euclidean gameplay and rendering; adds a genuinely different experience.

license.assets: Graphics drawn by the game's code; built-in font rendered from DejaVu Sans Bold (DejaVu fonts licence). Music and sounds are not included.

cover.alt: HyperRogue's Icy Land on the hyperbolic plane: the adventurer with a sword among seven-pointed ice walls, in a disc that shrinks towards its rim.

about: HyperRogue is a roguelike on the hyperbolic plane: every cell has seven neighbours, the world grows exponentially as you walk, and two steps the wrong way can lose you forever. Collect treasure across more than sixty lands, each with its own monsters, terrain and magic orbs, and reach the Orbs of Yendor in Hell.
This port builds HyperRogue's own web version from the pinned upstream source, unchanged, with saving switched back on. It runs entirely in your browser: no server and no account.

controlsSummary.action: Move towards it (attack by moving into a monster; use a ranged orb on a distant cell)
Help about what is there

controlsSummary.keys: h j k l y u b n · keypad
controlsSummary.action: Move in a screen direction
Wait a turn
Centre the view on you · rotate the view
Ranged orb (or strong wind) on the centre cell · drop a Dead Orb · crossbow fire mode · world overview
Always use a ranged orb there · orb inventory (Orb Strategy) · mark a mine (Minefield)
Quest status (and ending a game) · main menu · help · new game

Tap to move, slide to choose, long-press for help (as HyperRogue's mobile version); dock with centre, overview and quest, plus Aim (ranged orbs), Inspect, crossbow Fire, Drop, Orbs and Mark where they apply; thumb pad (wait in the centre)

knownLimitations: Not yet tested on physical iOS or Android devices; touch controls are verified in Chromium's mobile emulation only, and frame rate on phones is unmeasured (the game draws every frame on the page's main thread).
No music or sound effects (the web version has no audio).

As in HyperRogue itself, leaving ends the game in progress and records its score; a game can be continued later only if you leave while an Orb of Safety is powered, or in casual mode (the game's special modes menu).
Upstream's web version leaves out its translations and the 'shoot 'em up' mode.

compatibility.notes: Start, keyboard moves, the quest screen, message log, importing a desktop score file and keeping it across reloads verified by end-to-end tests (software WebGL, so frame rates there are not representative).

Dock, tap to move, long-press for help, Inspect mode and the thumb pad exercised by end-to-end tests (Aim, Fire, Drop, Orbs and Mark need orbs or lands the tests cannot reach: unit-tested docks only); not a substitute for a real device.
Played on a physical iPhone (iOS Safari) in November 2026: playable, with the touch controls. Desktop Safari not yet tested.

games.title: NetHack
games.description: The genre-defining dungeon adventure, famous for how much it anticipates: almost anything you try has been thought of.
games.rationale: Genre-defining game; upstream maintains a WebAssembly build and a window interface the port answers.

license.assets: NetHack's own tiles (by Warwick Allison and others; NetHack General Public License); otherwise text in the browser's monospace font

about: NetHack is the dungeon adventure famous for how much it anticipates: descend through the Dungeons of Doom, survive Gehennom, retrieve the Amulet of Yendor and ascend. Almost anything you try has been thought of, and every death is final.

This port builds NetHack 5.0.0 with upstream's own WebAssembly build and its window interface, answered in the browser the way NetHack's terminal version draws: the map in text or with NetHack's own tiles, menus and messages as on a terminal. It runs entirely in your browser: no server and no account.
